Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "the North Quay volunteer transport group keeps a weekly rota for rides to the clinic, the library, and the food market. It has one small van and three volunteers who can drive it, and a few people who can only take phone calls or help with bags. Jo Bell does the rota from a desk at the community room, usually on Thursday afternoon. She prints one copy for the noticeboard and puts the same shifts in a shared spreadsheet. The paper copy is what some drivers look at first, because they do not all check the spreadsheet before a shift. This has not been a problem every week, but it means a change can be visible in one place before another.

The Tuesday morning clinic run was assigned to Jo, with pickup for Mr. Hale at 7:30. The van used for that run was Van 2, which Rowan Pike had brought back to the depot on Monday evening, just before six. He had been taking two insulated grocery bags out of the back, and checked the receipt while he was still beside the open door. Rowan locked the van after that, but he left the cabin lamp switched on. The lamp stayed on overnight, and the battery was discharged by morning. Rowan said later, “I left the light on when I was checking the receipt.” The garage volunteer checked the van at 7:10 and found that the battery would not start the engine. He also found the lamp still on. So the Tuesday delay came from the battery being drained by the cabin lamp, not from a missing key or a mix-up about which vehicle was booked.

Jo was at the depot at 7:05 and saw the problem when she tried the ignition. She called Asha Nair, who was listed as the backup driver for the afternoon, and asked if she could take Mr. Hale in her own car instead. Asha could do that, but she needed to collect the foldable step from the community room first. Jo phoned Mr. Hale at 7:17 and told him that the pickup would be later. He said, “I can wait in the lobby, but I need to be at the clinic before half past eight.” Jo wrote that time on the rota margin while they were still talking. She did not tell him that the original time would hold, because she did not yet know how long it would take to arrange another vehicle.

1. Tuesday’s changed pickup

Asha collected the step and reached Mr. Hale’s building at 8:05. Jo had put the clinic address and the entrance with the blue awning in a text, since Mr. Hale uses the side entrance when it is raining. It was not raining that morning, but he had asked the group to keep using that entrance because the main doors were heavy for him. Asha drove him in her own car, and the trip was logged against the Tuesday clinic shift rather than as a separate market ride. Mr. Hale arrived at the clinic at 8:22. The volunteer group’s log records the pickup at 8:05 and the arrival at 8:22; it does not record how long he waited inside before his appointment.

Jo changed the shared spreadsheet at 8:35, after Asha had called to say she was back in the neighborhood. The paper rota at the depot still showed Jo as the driver for Van 2, because no one had taken down the noticeboard copy before the morning trip. Jo crossed out her name and wrote Asha beside it, with “own car” in the margin. She used a blue pen because the black marker was in the locked cupboard. The correction could be read clearly, though the line for the vehicle number still said Van 2. That line referred to the scheduled vehicle, not the one Asha used, and Jo left it as it was rather than trying to squeeze another note into the box.

At the short volunteer check-in on Wednesday, Rowan explained what he remembered about Monday evening. He had taken out the bags, looked over the receipt, and locked the van without noticing the lamp. The garage volunteer’s check matched that account: the lamp was on and the battery was low. Rowan offered to take the first Friday shift, but Jo said she would leave that shift assigned to Martin until the rota was reviewed. She did not say whether Rowan would drive a later shift. The group has a rule that volunteers can offer swaps, while Jo updates the published rota only after both drivers confirm the change.

Jo said she felt embarrassed that the paper copy had not been updated before the clinic run, although the van problem itself was the reason the original trip could not go ahead as planned. “I may have assumed everyone would check the spreadsheet,” she said at the check-in. That was her impression, not something she had asked each driver about. Martin said he usually checks the paper copy when he is at the community room and the spreadsheet on his phone when he is away. Asha said she had seen the afternoon backup entry on the spreadsheet but had not looked at the printed rota that morning. They did not settle on a single way that every volunteer would check a change.

The group keeps a small vehicle notebook in the glove compartment, separate from the passenger log. The Monday entry lists Van 2’s return time as 5:52 and Rowan’s initials beside the note about the grocery bags. On Tuesday, the garage volunteer added the battery check and wrote that the cabin lamp was on when he opened the van. Jo copied the repair appointment into the notebook for Thursday at 9:00, while the passenger log remained unchanged apart from the note about Asha’s car. The community room cupboard also holds spare printed rotas, but the next blank copy is dated for the week beginning May 20.
